title: Your first crash, and the debugger
summary: A program crashes. Instead of guessing, use a real debugger — breakpoints, stepping, locals and the call stack — to find out exactly why.

steps.title: Run it and watch it fail

quiz.question: What happens when you run the program?
options: It prints all three lines: nuts, screws and bolts.
It prints `nuts: 80`, then crashes (Segmentation fault / access violation) without printing anything more.
It prints `screws: 0` because screws aren't in stock.
explanations: Look again — run it in a terminal and read the output carefully.
It compiles without errors or warnings. The compiler can't catch every bug — this one only shows up when the program runs.
Right. One line of output, then the operating system kills the process. The output tells you roughly *when* it died, but not *why*. That's the debugger's job.
There is no item called screws — so where would a 0 come from? Run it and see.

steps.title: Stop the program and look inside

quiz.question: When the program crashes in the debugger, what are the values of `name` and `item` in main's frame?
explanations: "nuts" was found and printed fine. The crash happens on the next iteration.

Exactly. `find_item` searched the whole vector, found no "screws", and returned `nullptr` — the address 0, which means "points at nothing". Then `item->quantity` tried to read memory at (nearly) address 0, which the OS doesn't allow.
The loop never gets that far — it dies on the second name.
If item held a valid address, `item->quantity` would work. Look at its value in the Variables panel.

steps.title: Fix the bug
hints: `find_item` is behaving as designed — `nullptr` is how it says "not found". The bug is the caller ignoring that possibility.
Before using `item->quantity`, check `if (item == nullptr)` and print the not-found message instead.
